author: ablokeimet
title: THE UKRAINE WAR
content:
This article first appeared in The Anvil Vol 12 No 3, published 30 June 2023.

After the fall of the USSR in 1991, Ukraine became independent. The United States promised Russia that NATO would not expand eastwards, but it didn’t take long for Uncle Sam to renege. Without a global rival to consider, and concerned to find a new mission for NATO after the end of the Cold War, successive US Presidents agreed to requests from most countries in Eastern Europe to join. As each individual new member sought security in NATO, the threat of NATO to Russia increased. In a world of competing States, security for one is bought at the expense of insecurity for its neighbours.

Independent Ukraine was a country split culturally and politically into two halves. Western Ukraine spoke Ukrainian and looked to build economic relations with the European Union, especially with Germany. Eastern Ukraine spoke Russian and looked to preserve its industrial integration with Russia. Corrupt oligarchs from the two factions alternated in power, while the working class was politically marginalised. In 2014, a protest movement against the Russian-leaning Viktor Yanukovych grew into the Maidan Uprising. Politically diverse at the beginning, it shifted to the Right after Fascists physically beat the Left into dropping their banners and ceasing propaganda. By late February, Yanuykovych’s party had deserted him and he fled. Pro-West corrupt oligarchs took charge.

Vladimir Putin, President of Russia, didn’t take kindly to the defeat of his client and, the next month, sent the Russian army to occupy Crimea. A sham plebiscite ratified its accession to Russia, though it is probable that a genuine plebiscite would have achieved the same result, albeit with a smaller majority. In April, unrest started in the Donbas, covering the two most eastern Ukrainian provinces. Though the leaders there may have been politically independent at the beginning, it didn’t take long before Russian soldiers and Russian guns turned them into puppets. A messy, low-level civil war started up, before largely petering out a year or so later.

In 2019, Volodymyr Zelenskyy was elected President on an anti-corruption platform. Though Russian-speaking and Jewish, he nevertheless pursued a pro-Western course, aimed at joining both the EU and NATO. By 2022, Putin had lost patience and ordered the Russian army to invade. The Ukrainian army, better motivated and better organised, fought the invasion to a standstill and later recaptured significant ground. A Ukrainian offensive started a few weeks ago. It is making progress, but very slowly against a Russian military that is heavily dug in. A revolt by the leader of the Wagner group, a company of mercenaries, recently exposed deep divisions within the Russian ruling class and weakened Putin’s position, perhaps seriously.

Anarchists don’t support the nation State or its military. We therefore oppose the provision of money, weapons or personnel to the military forces of any State. Here in Australia, we have a special responsibility to oppose the Australian military.

Instead of supporting national militaries, we advocate fighting the class struggle, a position which does not change purely because one State invades another. We oppose war production. We encourage desertion, draft resistance, selective sabotage and diversion of war materiel to the revolutionary movement.

An exception to opposing the war effort is that we do not oppose specific measures to protect cities from aerial attack from planes, drones and such like. An exception to draft resistance is that revolutionaries may submit to conscription in order to engage in anti-war activity within the military.

At the front, Anarchists encourage fraternisation and the refusal of offensive operations. In occupied territory, Anarchists should fight for leadership of the resistance. And finally, we maintain our position even if it leads to the defeat of the military forces of the State in which we live. If some other State invades Australia, we are prepared to see the State conquered and to conduct resistance against the occupier rather than contribute to the victory of the Australian State.

First and foremost, the Melbourne Anarchist Communist Group opposes the Russian invasion of Ukraine. We oppose NATO and call for its dissolution, but the desire of the Ukrainian Government to join it doesn’t justify what Putin is dishonestly calling a “special military operation”. The invasion, though …

author: Unknown
title: Ceyda Sungur: "Mekansal okuryazarlık içinde bulunduğumuz düzeni sorgulamayı gerektiriyor"
content:
Atölye BİA'nın 25-26 Temmuz’da gerçekleştirilen Mekansal Okuryazarlık Atölyesi'nin ilk gününde Ceyda Sungur, “Mekansal Okuryazarlığa Giriş” ve “Toplumsal Mekanın Üretimi” başlıklı iki oturum gerçekleştirdi. 


Sungur, ilk oturumda katılımcılarla birlikte mekansal okuryazarlığın ne anlama geldiğini tartıştı. Mekanı yalnızca fiziksel özellikleriyle değil, toplumsal hafıza, gündelik yaşam, sınıfsal ilişkiler ve kentteki dönüşümler üzerinden ele aldı. 


Katılımcılar, mekan ve hafıza ilişkisini farklı örnekler üzerinden inceledi. Binaların mimarları, kapı zilleri, kentsel dönüşümle küçülen evler ve mahallelerde değişen ticari yapılar bu örnekler arasındaydı. 


Tanıma, tanışma ve dönüştürme 


Sungur, mekansal okuryazarlığı “tanıma, tanışma ve dönüştürme” süreci olarak tarif etti. Bir mekanın fiziksel özelliklerini fark etmenin “tanıma” aşaması olduğunu söyledi. Mekanın taşıdığı toplumsal ilişkileri sorgulamaya başlamanın ise tanımayı “tanışmaya” dönüştürdüğünü anlattı. 


Sungur, mekansal okuryazarlığın kişinin kendi konumunu ve içinde bulunduğu toplumsal ilişkileri sorgulamasını da beraberinde getirdiğine dikkat çekti.  


Kendi sınıfsal pozisyonumuzu ve sınıfın tarihsel olarak kendi mekanını nasıl ürettiğini sorgulamaya başladığımızda bir dönüşüm sürecine giriyoruz. Edindiğimiz bilgi ve becerileri eleştirel düşünceden geçirerek bir yurttaşlık pratiğine dönüştürüyoruz. Kişinin içinde bulunduğu ve dönüştürmeye çalıştığı düzen içinde farklı bir özne haline gelmesini, buradaki adaletsizlikler üzerinden bir hak arama süreci başlatmasını da dönüştürme eylemi olarak tarif ediyorum. 


Sungur, bu çerçevede mekansal okuryazarlığın kişinin mekanla ve çevresindeki toplumsal ilişkilerle kurduğu ilişkiyi yeniden düşünmesine imkan verdiğini vurguladı. 


 


 


 


 


 


Bu gönderiyi Instagram'da gör


 


 


 


 


 


 


 


 


 


 


 


Atölye BİA (@atolyebia)'in paylaştığı bir gönderi


Mekan toplumsal ilişkilerle nasıl üretiliyor? 


Günün ikinci oturumu “Toplumsal Mekanın Üretimi” başlığıyla devam etti. Sungur, bu kez tartışmayı “Neden mekan değil de toplumsal mekan diyoruz?” sorusuyla açtı. 


Katılımcılar bu soruyu hafıza, sosyalleşme, eşitlik, güvenli alan ve farklı toplumsal grupların mekanla kurduğu ilişkiler üzerinden tartıştı. 


Sungur, mekanın yalnızca fiziksel bir alan olmadığını vurguladı. Toplumsal ilişkilerin mekan içinde kurulduğunu, bu ilişkilerin aynı zamanda mekanı dönüştürdüğünü anlattı. Böylece mekanın sürekli üretilen ve yeniden üretilen bir süreç olduğunu söyledi. 


Bu süreçte fiziksel çevrenin yanı sıra sosyoekonomik koşulların, kültürün, kimliğin, toplumsal cinsiyetin ve iktidar ilişkilerinin de rol oynadığını belirtti. Mekanı oluşturan bu düzeylerin birbirinden ayrı düşünülemeyeceğini aktardı. 


Kadınlar mekanı nasıl deneyimliyor? 


Oturumda mekanın toplumsal cinsiyete göre nasıl farklı deneyimlendiği de tartışıldı. Katılımcılar, evden sokağa ve işyerine uzanan gündelik deneyimlerden örnekler verdi. 


Tartışma sırasında ev içi emeğin mekanla ilişkisi de gündeme geldi. Sungur, kadınlara atfedilen toplumsal rollerin evin deneyimlenme biçimini de belirlediğine dikkat çekti: 


Kadınlara toplumsal olarak atfedilmiş rollerin en çok ve en görünmez şekilde gerçekleştiği yerlerden biri ev. Ev içi emek de bu gündelik pratiklerin bir parçası. Bu nedenle ev, kadınlar için daha fazla emek harcanan ve farklı deneyimlenen bir mekan haline geliyor.


Sungur, toplumsal cinsiyet ilişkilerinin işyerindeki deneyimleri de şekillendirdiğini söyledi. İşçi ve işveren arasındaki hiyerarşinin, kadınlara ve erkeklere atfedilen rollerle birleştiğinde bir baskı aracına dönüşebildiğini belirtti. 


Mekan kimin için tasarlanıyor? 


Sungur, mekanın nasıl planlandığı ve tasarlandığına da dikkat çekti. Kaldırımların genişliğinden kentte hareket etmeyi belirleyen standartlara kadar birçok kararın, hangi bedenlerin hesaba katıldığını gösterdiğini anlattı. 


Kaldırım örneği üzerinden “standart” kabul edilen bedenin kim olduğu tartışıldı. Kaldırımın tekerlekli sandalye kullanan birinin, elinde poşet taşıyan birinin ya da yan yana hareket eden iki kişinin kullanımına uygun olup olmadığı sorgulandı. 


Sungur, bu örneklerle mekanın tasarlanma biçiminin bazı bedenlerin hareketini kolaylaştırırken bazılarını sınırlandırabildiğine dikkat çekti. 


Bir domates bize ne anlatır? 


Sungur, oturumun devamında katılımcılarla gündelik bir nesneden yola çıkarak mekanın üretim süreçlerini sorgulamaya yönelik bir egzersiz yaptı.  …

author: Rein Tarinay
title: Canada-Philippines ‘strategic partnership’ for whom?
content:
Hundreds protest during Ferdinand Marcos Jr’s visit in Vancouver Canada (Photo by BAYAN BC)

“Security, development, and economic growth for whom? For whom is this going to serve? It always goes to big business, to bureaucrats, to corrupt government officials, to the same people it always goes to. And we have to expose this, because this is not economic growth, security and development of the people. This is further putting the people in precarious, dangerous, exploitative conditions in both Canada and the Philippines.”

TORONTO – During last year’s State of the Nation Address (SONA), Ferdinand Marcos Jr. did not mention the unequal trade and military agreements with the United States. For this year’s SONA, as he ties up with another foreign power, progressives anticipate that Marcos Jr. will frame the agreements as yet another “achievement” of his administration.

Early July, Marcos Jr. met with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Vancouver and announced the Canada-Philippines Strategic Partnership under the guise of “ deepening bilateral cooperation in trade, energy, defence, and tourism .” The two governments boasted of its people-to-people relationship and claimed it will benefit economic growth. But progressives in Canada ask, who is this really for?

A priority of the bilateral partnership is concluding negotiations on a Canada-Philippines Free Trade Agreement by the end of the year. The agreement states that Canada aims to expand agricultural and forest product exports to the Philippines where landgrabbing, extractive mining, and militarization result in the killings of farmers and human rights defenders, as per the reports of various human rights watchdogs.

In an interview with Bulatlat , Alison Matthews, chairperson of the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) in Canada, emphasized that the unequal trade agreements that Carney and Marcos Jr. signed and ongoing talks on declaration of intent only marks continued worsening human rights violations against the Filipino people.

“Canada headquarters over half of the world’s mining companies, and many of those companies operate in the country. B2 Gold, Oceanagold , and Barrick Gold , all have projects in the Philippines, with a long history of human rights violations, including having the AFP and state militia surrounding those mines, and killing land defenders, and displacing indigenous people. These projects contaminate the water and the soil, making soil unproductive for farming, and water undrinkable, so people are forced to leave,” they told Bulatlat.

“Security, development, and economic growth for whom? For whom is this going to serve? It always goes to big business, to bureaucrats, to corrupt government officials, to the same people it always goes to. And we have to expose this, because this is not economic growth, security and development of the people. This is further putting the people in precarious, dangerous, exploitative conditions in both Canada and the Philippines,” Matthews added.

The agreement also includes a Joint Declaration of Intent on Energy and Natural Resources Cooperation . While it is still under negotiation, it signals a clear push toward increased Canadian involvement in Philippine energy and resource extraction. A Joint Declaration of Intent on Labour and Migration was also signed without amendment and wording that protects and defends migrant workers on Canada’s employer-tied temporary foreign worker system, which has left many overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) vulnerable to precarious working conditions, exploitation and abuse.

All these agreements are happening alongside the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA).

Matthews underscored Canada’s complicity in fascist repression and exploitation of the people in the Philippines through militarization and weapons trade deals, through the SOVFA between Canada and the Philippines.

This year marks the first year that the Canadian military participated in the Balikatan war exercises further pushing Canada’s Indo-pacific strategy, which BAYAN Canada asserts would further entrench Filipinos to “militarization and state terrorism”.

“While millions of Filipinos suffer from extreme poverty, skyrocketing prices of oil, food and basic commodities,  unemployment, worsening hunger, and militarization, Marcos Jr. travels overseas to further strengthen military and economic agreements that open the Philippines to foreign plunder and intervention. These agreements are not for …

author: anred
title: 110 años de la huelga en el puerto de Ingeniero White: ¿quién recuerda a José Falcioni y Atiliano Pascual?
content:
El 23 de julio de 1907 amanecía en el Puerto Comercial con los obreros en huelga. Las casas de chapa y madera, muchas montadas sobre pilotes, fueron testigo del paso de los trabajadores hacia la Casa del Pueblo, un lugar propicio para deliberar y decidir cómo continuar con los reclamos. En la Subprefectura se recibe una orden precisa de su jefe, el comandante Astorga, que se encuentra en Bahía: “hay que capturar a los delincuentes”. Hay 700 personas congregadas dentro y fuera del edificio. La patrulla produce ocho descargas cerradas sobre la multitud. Hay numerosos detenidos y ocho heridos. Dos de ellos de gravedad van a fallecer en los días siguientes: Atiliano Pascual y José Falcioni. A partir de ese momento el paro en el puerto es total. La asamblea de la Federación Obrera decide un paro de 48 horas. Van a adherir los albañiles, los pintores, los carpinteros, los barraqueros, los cocheros de plaza, los mozos, dependientes del comercio y muchos empleados del Ferrocarril pese a las presiones de los gerentes. El 26 una gran manifestación de cinco mil personas se moviliza en una ciudad militarizada a la que han llegado tropas de refuerzo. En el puerto, la manifestación consigue la libertad de los presos.

Por Enrique Gandolfo (Secretario adjunto CTA Bahía Blanca-Coronel Dorrego), para FM de la Calle.


El 23 de julio de 1907 amanecía en el Puerto Comercial con los obreros en huelga. Las casas de chapa y madera, muchas montadas sobre pilotes, fueron testigo del paso de los trabajadores hacia la Casa del Pueblo, un lugar propicio para deliberar y decidir como continuar con los reclamos.


Bien temprano había acontecido un incidente y una pelea con dos capataces ingleses que no se plegaban al paro. Los reclamos eran varios: por la reincorporación de dos compañeros despedidos, por reducción de las horas de trabajo, por mejores salarios. Los estibadores agregaban uno propio: que las bolsas de cereal no pesaran más de 70 kilos.


En 1907 se hacían obras de ampliación del muelle del Ferrocarril Sur (de propiedad inglesa) y de edificios destinados a la Aduana y a la Subprefectura. Por aquellos años ya se exportaban un millón de toneladas de trigo anuales y de enero a marzo trabajaban 5 mil obreros.


Bahía Blanca tenía un intendente (Jorge Moore) y concejales pero curiosamente todos llamaban Lord Mayor a un señor inglés que luego compraría imponente casa en la avenida (hoy Alem 41). Mister Arthur Coleman era el Superintendente del Ferrocarril Sur. Además, tuvo en sus manos la administración de servicios fundamentales para la ciudad como la electricidad, los tranvías, el Mercado de Victoria, el gas y el agua, actividades vinculadas al mismo ferrocarril inglés.


Foto: Federico Randazzo


Preocupado también por los reclamos obreros, el hombre fue muchos años presidente de la Sociedad Protectora del Trabajo, una organización que propiciaba el trabajo “libre” para evitar las molestas huelgas sindicales. Es que además de ganarse el pan con su trabajo, los obreros tenían oídos receptivos para ideas que eran la materia prima de la conciencia: la de los socialistas y los anarquistas.


Aquella mañana en la Casa del Pueblo, el calor de las pasiones justicieras hacía olvidar el frío del invierno junto al mar. En la Subprefectura se recibe una orden precisa de su jefe, el comandante Astorga, que se encuentra en Bahía: “Hay que capturar a los delincuentes”. Hay 700 personas congregadas dentro y fuera del edificio. La patrulla produce ocho descargas cerradas sobre la multitud. Hay numerosos detenidos y ocho heridos. Dos de ellos de gravedad van a fallecer en los días siguientes: Atiliano Pascual y José Falcioni, un italiano de 30 años socio de la Sociedad Recreativa La Siempre Verde.


A partir de ese momento el paro en el puerto es total. En Bahía la Federación Obrera llama a una asamblea que se va a realizar en su local de Lamadrid 199. Al día siguiente muere Atiliano Pascual. Sus compañeros lo van buscar al hospital y lo llevan a pulso hasta el cementerio. Se inicia una una colecta para ayudar a las familias de las víctimas. La asamblea de la Federación Obrera decide un paro de 48 horas. Van a adherir los albañiles, los pintores, los carpinteros, los barraqueros, los cocheros de plaza, los mozos, dependientes del comercio y muchos empleados del Ferrocarril pese a las presiones de los gerentes.

author: Ash Sarkar
title: Burnham’s Vibe Shift Won’t Pay the Bills
content:
Andy Burnham’s been prime minister for nearly a week, and the post-Keir vibe shift is in full swing. Gone are the days of frowning at the camera and insisting Britain can’t have nice things; instead, we’re getting capped bus fares, 

VAT scrapped

 on household electricity bills, and a 

20% cut in business rates

 for pubs, clubs and music venues.


Though we’re very much in the high days of the honeymoon period, nobody can argue that Burnham hasn’t learned from Starmer’s political missteps. It’s not complicated: don’t come into government talking about all the things you can’t do to improve people’s lives, otherwise they’ll vote for someone who can actually do something with the power they’ve been given. Any win, even if it’s as small as £45 a year off energy bills, should get the town-crier treatment.


But the UK’s problems are numerous, and our tolerance for prime ministers (if recent history is any indication) limited. The real tests have yet to come.


Burnham has identified one of the ex-PM’s greatest failures: politics can’t survive indefinitely on the promise that competent people will administer decline more efficiently. Indeed, Darren Jones – former Treasury minister and Starmerite ultra – has done his best this week to revive the bad vibes of the old guard, pointing out that the (now nixed) digital ID rollout that was meant to pay for the VAT cut was 

actually itself unfunded

.


There’s little sign that Jones’ missives are being interpreted as much more than a resentful swipe at the new government. But it does set up an obstacle for the new prime minister. The Labour right are a vengeful, petty bunch; they’d happily snarl you up in negativity and  backbiting if it advances their little globule within the party, even if it comes at the expense of Labour’s national popularity. Burnham’s political career has been characterised by a marked distaste for factionalism, but not everybody in the PLP feels the same way.


Other conflicts loom for the government. Burnham and Miatta Fahnbulleh, the newly promoted energy secretary and close ally of Ed Miliband, will have to decide whether to 

expand drilling for oil and gas

 in the North Sea. As I mentioned in

last week’s Cortado

, Miliband’s opposition to increasing our dependence on fossil fuels prompted some of Labour’s trade union backers to publicly denounce him as a “noose around the neck” of job creation, even going so far as to imply that the MP for Doncaster is anti-working class.


Fahnbulleh, for one, has changed her tune. Back when she worked for a left-ish NGO in 2023, she 

signed a letter

 which blasted new fossil fuel projects as “irresponsible and shortsighted”. But this week, she was an evangelist for “

pragmatism

”, and pointedly made a visit to Aberdeen. The choice in front of her is to stick to her principles, and piss off two of the country’s biggest trade unions, or allow for expanded drilling on Jackdaw and Rosebank, and thus open up space for the Greens to hammer Labour on climate change.


New relationship energy isn’t a renewable resource. By definition, it will run out. A vibe shift is both powerful and insubstantial: we all know when we’re feeling different, but that’s not necessarily a transformation in political reality. Stephen Bush in the FT has branded Burnham’s initial raft of announcements “

Continuity Reevesnomics

” – while you might get a few sunny headlines out of cutting VAT on electricity, it’s not actually going to make a big dent in the cost of living.


Unless or until Andy Burnham makes a big policy intervention – which would put him on a collision course with the rightwing flank of his own party – at some point, voters are going to notice that they’re not much better off than they were under Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves.

author: Unknown
title: How Letter Carriers Can Organize to Prevent Smoke Injury
content:
Letter carriers and other people who work outdoors, especially in the upper Midwest and East, are experiencing hazardous levels of smoke from Canadian wildfires. Some areas have been experiencing AQI (Air Quality Index) measurements of over 300, even over 500, with local authorities advising residents to stay indoors.


As temperatures continue to rise from climate change and vegetation dries out and catches fire from lightning, this situation will get worse.


We are being given advice by Postal Service management and our union leadership to make individual decisions about whether we are safe delivering mail in these conditions. Wrong! We are berated with the slogan “Safety Depends on Me!” Wrong!


Management should be following local health advisories and keep carriers off the street in these conditions. But reports from carriers all over the Midwest let us know that management is instructing carriers to deliver the mail and use a mask if desired and available. Wrong!


Many carriers will follow management instructions despite concern for their own or co-workers’ safety because they fear management retaliation if they do not—especially people in the more vulnerable job categories of City Carrier Associates and Part-Time Flexible employees.


Or they assume that they will not be impacted by the smoke. (Hint: wildfire smoke inhalation can damage healthy individuals over time; see the last section of this article.)


Or they do not want to be considered weak when others are going ahead. Or they don’t want to bring back mail to have to face overburdened days to come.


THE ANSWER: COLLECTIVE ACTION


What is to be done? Collective action to protect all carriers, together, in the area. Here’s a step-by-step approach:


Educate carriers on their right to refuse to work outdoors when there is serious smoke from wildfires,

 using stand-up meetings, flyers, bulletin boards, and breakroom meet-ups.


The criterion for when mail delivery is unsafe is

not

 only when there is a “risk of death or serious bodily injury.”


We have the right to avoid

any

 illness or injury caused by unsafe air quality, which can be predicted by Air Quality Index and is scientifically proven (see the last section of this article).


Even the USPS directives, distributed as stand-ups in late July, state, “Those who are most at risk are… active people of all ages who exercise or work vigorously outdoors…”


Demand (by circulating a petition or speaking up at a stand-up meeting) that management supply every carrier with an N95 or P100 mask.

 If necessary, use multiple 1767 Hazardous Condition and Article 14 Safety and Health grievances with evidence from local authorities or nearby AQI readings.


Get all carriers in your station or your area on a WhatsApp chat.


Assign carriers to monitor air quality index

 (AQI at

AirNow.gov

) and keep track of local authorities’ directives.


Decide together (consulting AirNow.gov) how the group should respond to certain AQI levels,

 i.e. when to refuse to go out without N95 or P100 masks, when carriers with respiratory conditions should bring the mail back, when everyone should bring the mail back, etc.


Talk through the consequences if everyone brings the mail back.

 Will management discipline all of us? Can we threaten to go public if they try? What if mail piles up and takes a while to get delivered?


When alerted by the monitors, spread the word of AirNow.gov advice and indicate that “many carriers may want to” bring the mail back.

 Prepare carriers for these words that allow “plausible deniability,” i.e. you are not calling for a strike, only for carriers to be safe.


When bringing the mail back, fill out form 1767 (hazardous conditions) describing the specific hazardous conditions

 (e.g. AQI and/or local authority directives).


Also fill out form 1571 (undelivered mail) describing the mail curtailed. Inform management that you will not work outside but that you are available to work inside. Do not leave until your shift is over or until directed by management (fill out form 3971 for Administrative Leave).


HEALTH RISKS OVER TIME


Wildfire smoke inhalation can damage healthy individuals over time. The smoke contains a high concentration of fine particulate matter and toxic pollutants. These ultrafine particles penetrate deep into the lungs, enter the bloodstream, and trigger systemic inflammation and oxidative stress, which can lead to cumulative cardiovascular and respiratory risks, as …

content:
Una nueva protesta de jubilados, esta vez con el acompañamiento de las tres centrales (CGT y las CTAs), elevó el piso de participación que se realiza miércoles tras miércoles. De la jornada también participaron movimientos sociales y organizaciones de izquierdas y de vertiente peronista.

En el marco de una gran jornada de lucha y movilización en todo el territorio nacional, que

comenzó a la mañana con la movilización de organizaciones sociales y piqueteras contra el cierre del programa Volver al Trabajo

, delegaciones de sindicatos de las tres centrales obreras de la República Argentina se hicieron presentes en la ronda de jubiladas y jubilados de todos los miércoles.


Entre ellas hubo gremios que asistieron, quizás, por primera vez, y otros como La Bancaria, ATE y Camioneros que además de estar presentes con una columna importante, son participantes frecuentes. Y, en el caso de los conducidos por Moyano, asisten a las y los jubilados con ollas populares cada miércoles. Es un gesto de solidaridad que aporta a la lucha y permite que muchos de los manifestantes puedan contar con una comida caliente, que se suma al aporte de los hinchas y algunos otros gremios, que vienen reuniendo y distribuyendo alimentos en las rondas.

La jornada del miércoles dejó varios aspectos para destacar. En primer lugar, se registró una importante participación tanto del sector peronista como de las organizaciones de izquierda, lo que evidenció un amplio espectro político confluyendo en el reclamo. Sin embargo, más allá de la diversidad política, lo que realmente convoca a muchos adultos mayores fue la urgencia alimentaria.


Según relató el Chaca, referente de los jubilados, las organizaciones están realizando un esfuerzo para cubrir al menos dos comidas al mes por persona, a través de la entrega de bolsones de alimentos. En ese sentido, destacó que cada vez es más frecuente la presencia de jubiladas y jubilados que antes no participaban de las movilizaciones y que ahora asisten exclusivamente para buscar el bolsón de comida.

Otro dato que surgió de la jornada fue la amplia participación de la juventud: jóvenes de veinte y pico de años, tanto varones como mujeres. Este colectivo, si sigue creciendo y se consolida, puede perfilarse como un actor clave para sostener la lucha en el tiempo.


Todo esto ocurre en un contexto de profunda crisis para el sector. Las y los jubilados atraviesan una situación crítica signada por el congelamiento de los bonos – en $70.000- y el aumento permanente de la canasta básica. Para julio de 2026, la jubilación mínima con bono ronda los $481.948, tras una actualización del 2,1%, muy por debajo de la inflación real. A esto se suma una caída del 50% en las nuevas altas previsionales, lo que profundiza el desamparo de quienes intentan acceder al sistema. El ajuste también golpea las atenciones del PAMI y la entrega de medicamentos, dos pilares fundamentales para la salud de los adultos mayores.

author: Maira Escardovelli
title: Tarifaço: Como a medida de Trump divide trabalhadores e empresários do setor de calçados
content:
No dia seguinte ao anúncio do governo norte-americano sobre a nova

tarifa

 de 25% imposta a produtos brasileiros, a Confederação Nacional da Indústria (CNI) divulgou uma nota manifestando “extrema preocupação” com a medida. Segundo a entidade, o tarifaço agrava um cenário já pressionado e “amplia a insegurança para empresas” do Brasil e dos Estados Unidos. Os cálculos são de que, após o anúncio da primeira sobretaxa em 2025, as exportações de companhias brasileiras diminuíram 13%, uma queda de 2,6 bilhões de dólares.


A Federação das Indústrias do Estado de São Paulo (FIESP), liderada por Paulo Skaff, lamentou a medida, sob a justificativa de que a nova tarifa impacta “significativamente a competitividade do país perante concorrentes globais”. A Abicalçados, que representa a indústria calçadista, um dos setores afetados, também revisou sua projeção para o ano, calculando uma queda média de 7,1% nas exportações do produto, o dobro do previsto antes da sobretaxa.


O presidente da entidade, Haroldo Ferreira, esteve, inclusive, em reunião com integrantes do governo federal nesta terça-feira, 21 de julho, em Brasília, para discutir propostas para diminuir o impacto no setor calçadista, que detém cerca de 280 mil empregos no Brasil. Na mesa de negociação, a possibilidade de concessão de linhas de crédito e de menor custo para a indústria, além da ampliação do retorno da alíquota sobre produtos exportados pelo país. Além da Abicalçados, estiveram com o governo a Associação Brasileira da Indústria de Máquinas e Equipamentos (Abimaq) e representantes dos setores da indústria automotiva, de plástico e eletrônica.


Abicalçados, que reúne as indústrias do setor, aumentou a projeção de queda nas exportações em 2026 para 7,1%


A aflição do empresariado, entretanto, não encontra eco entre os trabalhadores do chão de fábrica. Ao menos não do setor de calçados. Segundo apurou a

Agência Pública

,

sindicatos e associações de duas das principais regiões produtoras de sapatos para exportação do país, Rio Grande do Sul e interior paulista (representado pela cidade de Franca) avaliam que, na realidade, “não há motivo para desespero

”, uma vez que as empresas do segmento já encontraram, há algum tempo, outros caminhos para além da venda aos Estados Unidos. Um deles foi o acordo de livre comércio do Mercosul com a União Europeia, que passou a valer de forma provisória em maio deste ano.


“Desde os primeiros sinais [do tarifaço] que foi dado pelos Estados Unidos, as empresas que exportam não têm 100% de trabalho de exportação. Elas exportam só uma parte do produto”, explica João Nadir Pires, presidente da Federação dos Trabalhadores nas Indústrias do Calçado e do Vestuário do Estado do Rio Grande do Sul.

“Claro que faz falta, mas as empresas já estão preparadas com as suas inteligências, com seus analistas de mercado, procurando já há tempos outros caminhos”

, completa.


Entre os mercados que aparecem como solução, de acordo com Nadir, estão a Colômbia, Peru, Equador e a própria Argentina, que, segundo dados da Abicalçados, é o segundo principal destino do calçado brasileiro. Relatório da mesma entidade mostra, inclusive, que as exportações brasileiras de calçados em 2025, 2024 e 2023 tiveram a vizinha Argentina como principal comprador em volume, com 13,7 milhões de pares e participação de 13,2% do total exportado no ano passado. A preocupação maior, segundo João, é a concorrência com a China.


Por que isso importa?


Além do Brasil, taxado em 25%, os EUA anunciaram tarifas extras de 50% aos produtos do Canadá

Também entraram na “punição” norte-americana países como Indonésia, México e Paquistão, mas com taxas menores, de 10%.


Para o presidente do Sindicato dos Trabalhadores nas Indústrias de Calçados de Franca, Wellington Paulo de Oliveira, o tarifaço também não inicia um movimento de possíveis demissões. Segundo ele, acontece outro problema na cidade, que é o segundo maior polo calçadista do Estado de São Paulo, com 28,7% da produção: falta mão de obra especializada, que geralmente têm migrado para empregos no setor de construção civil.


Já na avaliação do economista-chefe da Federação das Indústrias do Estado do Rio Grande do Sul, Giovani Baggio, as demissões do setor já estão ocorrendo. Ele cita os resultados do CAGED, do governo federal, que mostram que, até o acumulado de 2026, a indústria do segmento de couro e calçados no Rio Grande do Sul perdeu 3.382 postos de trabalho.

author: Ruby Healer
title: Hanson is hardening up a far-right base—we need to organise against her
content:
When Marine Le Pen stepped in to replace her Holocaust-denying father as leader of the French National Front in 2011, it was part of a strategy to cleanse the far-right party of associations with Nazism. Le Pen judged that distancing herself from overt racism was the only practical route to electability. The French dubbed this manoeuvre

dédiabolisation

 (“de-demonisation”).

Fifteen years later, Australia’s homegrown far right is moving in exactly the opposite direction. Pauline Hanson—a creature who initially slithered out of the Australian conservative tradition as a Liberal candidate in 1996—now openly calls for cultural homogenisation and actively seeks out the company of prominent neo-Nazis.

Hanson is making no attempt to sanitise her politics for the sake of broad appeal. On the contrary, she is hardening her political positions, becoming more unapologetically fascistic, and encouraging her supporters to follow.  

If anything, the more “official” endorsement Hanson receives—by way of National Press Club invitations,

corporate donations

 and ex-Liberal backing—the more brazenly she pushes her extremist agenda. Political commentators are baffled by her apparent inability to judge what might hurt or help her “broad appeal”, but they misunderstand. 

She couldn’t care less if One Nation’s positions are unpopular (otherwise she would not promote abortion bans, campaign for fossil fuels and oppose parental leave payments). Hanson is advancing a conscious political argument, aimed at disaffected coalition voters: that Australian conservatism needs to become more confident and more extreme. She deliberately flouts every

cordon sanitaire

 that is supposed to separate “acceptable” mainstream conservatism from its mutant far-right offspring. Her aim is to create a hard, right-wing base that can be mobilised when necessary and used to push mainstream political discourse further to the right.

It was only last month that off-the-rails

Nine News

 presenter Karl Stefanovic was sacked for podcasting with UK fascist street agitator Tommy Robinson—a signal from the Australian media establishment about what they currently consider outside of acceptable discourse.

But just weeks later, Hanson is revelling in the opportunity to associate with Robinson, joining him for an hour-long podcast interview and walking tour through London’s multiracial neighbourhoods as well as his home town of Luton. “I don’t feel like I’m in England”, Hanson told Robinson in a video shared on his TikTok channel. “I definitely don’t want Australia to become like this.”

Hanson used the podcast as a platform to expand on the theme of “monoculture” introduced in her National Press Club address in June. She explained to Robinson that new arrivals entering Australia today are “different” from European migrants who settled after the Second World War. Those people “really assimilated” and “learned to speak English”, she said.

Robinson chimed in that he’d seen “some crazy videos” highlighting levels of Pakistani and Somali (i.e. non-white) migration to Australia. “How have you ended up with ... all of these African problems, with violent Africans?”

Hanson answered that it all “started” when the White Australia policy ended in 1973—“then they started bringing in the different migrants”. She then launched into a racialised anti-welfare tirade accusing Muslims in particular of moving to Australia “purely for the welfare system”.

The obvious implication is that, for Hanson, white immigrants are okay (as long as they speak only English), and everyone else is not welcome. This is the “monoculture” to which she wants to subject us; this is the hellish “one nation” she seeks to build.

Such open white supremacist politics is, for now, still rejected by majority establishment opinion—even Nigel Farage (Reform UK leader) refuses to engage with white nationalists like Robinson, preferring to target foreign “culture” rather than biological race and ethnicity. And Liberal Party leader Angus Taylor likewise criticised Hanson for appearing with Robinson.

But Hanson is far from being out on a limb. Rather she joins a growing camp of explicit ethno-nationalists who are cohering on the international right. In Britain, MP Rupert Lowe has split away from Reform to set up Restore Britain—a rival electoral outfit that YouGov

estimates

 is winning over at least 10 percent of Farage’s voter base. According to anti-fascist research centre Hope Not Hate, Restore …

author: Evan Vorpahl
title: Kansas Amendment Battle Highlights Billionaires’ Efforts to Capture State Courts
content:
Charles Koch and Leonard Leo’s hands are all over a ballot measure to change how judges get on the Kansas Supreme Court.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The networks of two major players who helped capture the U.S. Supreme Court — anti-abortion lawyer Leonard Leo and oil billionaire Charles Koch — have also long targeted state courts to advance their regressive agenda. One of their tactics, influencing the way that state justices are selected nationwide, is being borne out in Kansas.

On August 4, voters in Kansas will decide the fate of a state constitutional amendment placed on the ballot by the Republican legislature. Four major groups involved in campaigns around the amendment have raised nearly $12 million, according to the Sunflower State Journal . If the amendment succeeds, it would replace Kansas’s historic merit selection process for selecting state supreme court justices with direct elections. Despite trying to convince voters that the amendment would be a win for democracy, dark money groups and their backers are supporting the ballot initiative as a way to further expand their own special interest influence and open the door to bigger spending in the state’s selection of judges.

Koch’s Americans for Prosperity (AFP) has heavily pushed the amendment campaign with digital ads and get-out-the-vote efforts in support of the amendment. A new front tied to Leo’s network has also been flooding the airwaves with ads, rewriting history by claiming that when Kansans elected their judges, “ it worked well .” Their PR effort ignores the fact that Kansans originally voted to reform the appointment process to require merit-based selection as part of the state’s constitution because of widespread public outrage over an infamous court selection scandal in the 1950s.

State courts often serve as a check on far right state legislative majorities captured by special interests — the last line of governmental defense against powerful political forces seeking to eliminate people’s rights and freedoms at the state level. Since the early 2000s, Leo has been attacking merit-based judicial appointment systems , mounting a substantial assault next door in Missouri in 2005, as True North documented . Merit selection systems, like the one in Kansas, promote the selection of judicial candidates based on their qualifications, rather than their political views or support from special interests. Kansas has already seen a decade-long effort by the far right to chip away at the independence of the state judiciary in response to its rulings about how the Kansas constitution protects access to abortion and requires public school funding.

Currently, Kansas Supreme Court justices are appointed by the governor, who selects from a slate of three qualified candidates recommended by a nonpartisan nominating commission. The commission is composed of four attorneys selected by the state bar, four non-attorneys appointed by the governor, and one attorney selected by a statewide vote of legal professionals. This process is transparent and still depends on voters supporting the retention of a justice after their first year on the bench. The merit-based system is also widely considered effective in limiting politics from the appointment process and insulating judges from political backlash over rulings.

State voters enshrined merit selection for Kansas’s Supreme Court Justices in the Constitution in 1958 in response to the notorious “triple play” scandal , in which outgoing Republican Gov. Fred Hall devised a scheme to get himself installed as Chief Justice of the Kansas Supreme Court during his last few weeks in office. Until 2013, judges on the Kansas Court of Appeals were also selected via merit, but then-Republican Gov. Sam Brownback and his allies in the legislature repealed the law for the state intermediate appellate court; shortly after, Brownback appointed his former chief legal counsel Caleb Stegall to the Court of Appeals.

The national right-wing interests advancing this amendment have been cloaking their support with misleading claims that it would advance democracy in the Sunflower state. The reality is that this amendment has long been sought by right-wing billionaires and political operatives, because it will open the door to a wave of spending designed to capture the court, which has stood in the way of their agenda to criminalize abortion, defund …

title: Call for a nationwide demonstration on Saturday 25 July 2026 in Argos in response to the police-perpetrated, racist murder of Theodoros (Greece)
content:
‘They killed him. Now his little body is kept alive only by machines, and he has seven bullets in his head. He was killed in a very brutal manner. The doctors say that bullets were used which are banned for the police. Those bullets explode inside the body as they pass through. The doctors removed two bullets; three remain in his brain. He’s suffering from external and internal bleeding and has two huge holes on one side and the other. I can’t see the back. Three bullets exploded and shattered into tiny pieces inside. And it happened – you know what happened… it turned to mush inside. I think his brain stopped working.”
The words of Theodoros’s mother about her murdered son.

Thodoris Zavradinos Karambampas from Argos was seriously injured in the early hours of Wednesday 8 July 2026 by police gunfire, as officers from the Special Anti-Crime Unit (OPKE) pursued him and ultimately executed him because he failed to stop at a traffic checkpoint whilst driving his car. Thodoris was on the autism spectrum and had an 89 per cent disability, according to his mother. He passed away following a four-day battle in the intensive care unit at KAT hospital in Athens late on Saturday evening, 11 July 2026.
We live in an age where state-sanctioned killings and workplace accidents are an everyday occurrence. Both in Argos and in every town across Greece, the struggling community must take the lead, organise its resistance against police violence, state repression, fascist gangs, employers’ arbitrariness and workplace accidents, and defend the interests of the people, the youth and our class.

Everyone on Saturday 25 July at 12:00 am for the nationwide demonstration, with a pre-rally at Agios Petros Square (Argos Museum).

Through the economic destitution it has brought upon our lives, the killings of workers, the killings of migrants at the borders, the violence of patriarchy (which we saw unfold in its most brazen form during the trial for the rape at Omonia police station), the attacks, torture and killings by the police, as well as its very stance in deliberately allowing a hunger striker to die and actively participating in the genocide of the Palestinians.

author: By Aris Dimitrakopoulos, Contributor
title: As Senegal Cracks Down on LGBTQ Rights, Activists Seek Help From Abroad
content:
“I prefer to remain anonymous because of the authorities in Senegal,” Mamadou, one of the founders of the Senegalese LGBTQ rights organization Free Senegal, told Unicorn Riot. Speaking under an alias, Mamadou agreed to speak with Unicorn Riot only if he could remain anonymous. He fled the country in 2021 after years of harassment and is one of many now worried for their safety amid a wave of anti-LGBTQ repression that took hold this year.


His fears are not unfounded. Since February, Senegalese authorities have initiated a crackdown against the LGBTQ community, reportedly arresting hundreds across the country. Local newspapers announce new arrests every week, including of celebrities.


The recent crackdown started after the dismantling of a suspected French-Senegalese pedophilia ring in early February. It culminated with Parliament passing a new anti-LGBTQ law by an overwhelming majority in March, which doubled prison sentences for “acts against nature” to up to 10 years.


Under this provision, the law equates same-sex relationships with sexual crimes such as bestiality and necrophilia. Furthermore, in a separate article, it stipulates a sentence of up to seven years in prison for the “promotion or financing” of homosexuality, bisexuality, or transgender identity.


According to Free Senegal, at least 184 members of the LGBTQ community have been detained and jailed as of early April. “Those who are not detained are trying to flee the country because they are afraid for their security. There is a mass exodus,” said Mamadou.


“All community leaders have left, members of organizations have left. There are currently no allies of the community in Senegal,” he added.


Mamadou describes an atmosphere of panic where LGBTQ individuals are being arrested after being reported to the police, often by those close to them or identified after authorities search the phones of detainees. Even lawyers are hesitant to take their cases for fear of being targeted themselves. 


Due to this restrictive environment, LGBTQ individuals in Senegal have to turn to either informal support networks or organizations outside Senegal for help. One of them is the Canadian LGBTQ rights organization Rainbow Railroad, which provides assistance to persecuted LGBTQ individuals around the world.


According to Chief Programs Officer Devon Matthews, the organization, until early April had already received 90 requests for help from Senegalese citizens, a sharp increase compared to 2025, when it received 106 the whole year. The number of requests followed domestic developments, with a spike in early March during the discussion and voting on the law.


The organization does not have an on-the-ground presence in Senegal, however, it is drawing from its experience in

Uganda

 and other African countries to assist the community in the country.


Uganda’s Death Sentence on its LGBTI+ Communities

 [2023]


“We’re trying to focus most of our efforts right now internally on the activists and organizations that we are aware of, some of whom are reaching out to us directly,” said Matthews, adding that Rainbow Railroad is providing limited financial assistance, helping connect activists with one another and offering support with information and logistics.


“Right after these laws are passed, certain activists are [being] targeted or [put] on government lists. What we want to do is just make sure that those activists are able to either temporarily leave or move from the city to a quieter area while the dust from the law settles,” she said. “That’s the first request that we often get.”


Matthews adds that although Rainbow Railroad is able to refer 250 LGBTQ refugees each year directly to the Canadian government for resettlement in Canada, the program is reserved only for the most vulnerable of individuals who have already fled to a third country and the process takes years.


While Senegalese activists are trying to avoid arrest and persecution, those who campaigned in favor of the anti-LGBTQ law have allies in the highest echelons of the parliamentary majority party, PASTEF. Its leader, Senegal’s former prime minister, Ousmane Sonko, pledged to impose tougher penalties for homosexuality during the 2024 election campaign.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: A new hunting season has been declared (pt. 2), or the normalisation of fascism
content:
On the 16th of July, at the invitation of Marco Rubio and the US State Department, representatives of over 60 countries

gathered

 to hear Rubio

annonce

 that “the counterterrorism architecture of the free world, built over a generation against jihadist mass murder, should be rebuilt and aimed at the domestic left”, wherever it might show itself, for “the left”, in its many incarnations, is the implacable enemy of the “West” and its civilization.


This is a distinctive and unique evil.  It has always been driven by a hatred above all else, a hatred for civilization itself.  It is a revolt of the worst against the best, a revolt of the weak and the cowardly against the strong and the good.  It is perpetrated by those who cannot build, who cannot create, who cannot achieve great things, and take their revenge upon the world for their own inadequacy by seeking to destroy those who can.  This is what radical leftism is.  It may wear various different slogans and ideologies across place and time.  They can call themselves anti-capitalist or anti-imperialist or communist or anarchist or Marxist.  But the fundamental character is always the same.  It’s always the same. 


It is a poisonous resentment cloaked in the language of equality and justice and liberation, an overwhelming need to tear down what greater men have built, to wreck what is beautiful and what is right on behalf of people who are only filled with ugliness and have nothing else to offer the world.  Through violence and through terror, they once again seek to impose their ugliness on all of us.  The old dogma was wrong.  The old dogma was wrong; none of this is driven by idealism.  It is not utopian.  In fact, it is the opposite. 


If the threat comes from “within”, the “left” is nevertheless “transnational”, with financial and ideological support coming from countries such as Iran and

Cuba

. (“Cuba’s assault on the United States was never, at root, a quarrel over economic policy or sovereignty or even ownership of a particular territory. … It was a revolution against western civilisation itself – waged, in part, via the novel and insidious method of persuading the children of the west to turn against their own inheritance. … Today, Cuban agents and operatives maintain a foothold in hundreds of front groups, activist organisations, solidarity centres, and ideological NGO and nonprofit networks. These groups collectively represent one of the single largest, most sophisticated and dangerous vectors for hostile foreign influence in modern American history.” –  from

Cuba: Capital of 21st-Century Communism

, published by the US state department, July 20, 2026. The report blames Havana for everything from “the George Floyd riots to the rise of antifa to the explosion of pro-terrorist activism on American college campuses”) In other words, if the “indigenous left” of the USA is fundamentally a threat, it is ultimately a foreign, un-American threat which must be dealt with on a global scale through the construction of a new, “anti-leftist” global order.


After Rubio’s intervention, the stage was given to the White House deputy chief of staff, Steven Miller, whose

words

 unveiled a much more radical vision.


It’s very important to understand that left-wing political terrorism seeks as its ultimate end the overthrow of our system and form of government. … 


Left-wing terrorism always ends in bloodshed, misery, and suffering.  It only can travel in one direction.  There’s no point at which the left-wing terrorist is satisfied with his gains and ceases progressing.  Inevitably, left to run its course, it always becomes a gulag.  It always becomes the mass imprisonment of political enemies, the stripping of their rights and freedoms, inflicting immense pain, humiliation, suffering in order to establish complete and total control – control through psychological and physical and actual terror.  And we have to understand that that is the scope and the extent of the threat that we face. 


As Secretary Rubio also pointed out, this is an international network.  Antifa, as an example, operates in dozens of countries all throughout the world.  They share common networks of funding and organization and information sharing.  And so, all of our intelligence agencies and law enforcement entities should be collaborating and coordinating and working together in order to root out these organizations.

title: Miguel Amorós - L’importance actuelle de la Colonne de Fer dans la mémoire de la révolution espagnole
content:
Archive Textes Auteur·e·s Sujets Mots-clés Derniers ajouts Ajouter à la bibliothèque

Applications pour appareils mobiles

La réforme convenue du franquisme qui a donné naissance au régime actuel, qualifié de « démocratie » par ses administrateurs, s’est fondée sur l’oubli le plus absolu non seulement du génocide qui a suivi la victoire de Franco dans la guerre, mais aussi de la contre-révolution républicaine qui l’a facilitée. De ce fait, l’histoire récente a été occultée par un pacte de silence entre les héritiers de la Dictature et ceux de la République. Entre les enfants des assassins de Lorca et les descendants de ceux qui ont tué Nin. L’amnésie a servi à légitimer le nouveau régime hybride né en 1977 ; c’est pourquoi le rétablissement véritable de la mémoire devrait inexorablement conduire à sa délégitimation. L’actuel parti de l’ordre fait tout son possible pour que cela ne se produise pas, habillant la mémoire avec un costume fait sur mesure. Ce sont toujours les vainqueurs qui écrivent l’Histoire. Mais aucune loi de « mémoire historique » ne pourra réconcilier la barbarie passée avec le présent oublieux, ni jamais intégrer le passé révolutionnaire dans l’ordre établi post-franquiste, à moins de le convertir en crime, tâche à laquelle s’attelle actuellement une poignée d’historiens complices. Mon livre [ La Columna de Hierro , Ed. Milvus] relève du point de vue inverse, celui des perdants, dont beaucoup ont payé de leur vie le prix de la défaite. Là seulement on trouvera la vérité.

La guerre civile espagnole n’était pas une simple confrontation entre la « démocratie » et le « fascisme », comme le prétendent souvent les historiens progressistes, dont l’imaginaire exclut la lutte des classes. C’est avant tout une révolution ratée qui s’est déroulée dans un contexte international marqué par une formidable crise économique et la montée des totalitarismes. Elle s’est déroulée sur deux fronts, et là se situe cette caractéristique que l’on veut à tout prix cacher ou déformer : à l’avant-garde, contre les fascistes et les rebelles militaires, et à l’arrière, contre la révolution prolétarienne. Le 19 juillet 1936, la classe ouvrière s’est vue obligée de descendre dans les rues de nombreuses villes et villages espagnols pour affronter le coup d’État militaire, quasiment à mains nues. L’État espagnol amorphe s’est effondré du jour au lendemain. Lorsque cela se produisit, le prolétariat tenta d’appliquer les changements sociaux qu’il réclamait depuis longtemps. En effet, le soulèvement clérical-militaire-fasciste déclencha une révolution, spontanée, la plus profonde qu’il n’y ait jamais eue, qui impulsa un type original de transition de la liberté vers le communisme à travers des procédures communales de production et de distribution. Les colonnes miliciennes furent sa première réalisation défensive. Dans les premiers jours, l’initiative revint aux ouvriers et aux paysans de toutes tendances, qui prirent d’assaut les casernes, exproprièrent les terres et les bâtiments, occupèrent les usines et les terres agricoles avec l’intention de les collectiviser, prirent en charge l’ordre public et organisèrent des milices avec les armes qu’ils purent récupérer dans les armureries et les casernes. La révolution était dans les rues, et personne ne la dirigeait. Dans ces moments, seuls l’improvisation, l’audace et le courage étaient à l’œuvre. Il y avait une unité qui, dès sa naissance, façonna son caractère, avec une personnalité si marquée qu’elle se détacha du côté antifasciste. La Colonne de Fer, formée par des militants valenciens de la CNT-FAI dans le but de libérer Teruel, impulsa, partout où elle passait, les idéaux d’égalité, de liberté et de justice sociale, fondements de la future société à construire sur les piliers de la raison et du travail. Mais alors que l’enthousiasme révolutionnaire se répandait sur les parapets et dans les villages proches du front, il se refroidit dans l’arrière-garde valencienne. Voyons pourquoi.

Valence était différente de la Catalogne, de la Castille ou de l’Aragon. Dans la région du Levant, après la réunification [1] , le secteur modéré « trentiste », ouvertement réformiste et accommodant, était beaucoup plus fort, et ses relations avec la franc-maçonnerie et la politique conventionnelle étaient notoires. Le secteur radical était minoritaire, soutenu par peu de syndicats, quelques fédérations locales de villages ruraux et une poignée de jeunes gens fougueux des groupes et des athénées …

Zusammen kämpfen gegen Feminizide und Nazigewalt!

Der Mord an Beate Fischer


Am Abend des 23. Juli 1994 wurde Beate Fischer in Reinickendorf von einer Gruppe Neonazis misshandelt, vergewaltigt und ermordet. Über ihr Leben ist wenig bekannt. Sie war 32 Jahre alt, als sie starb, lebte damals in Weißensee und war Mutter zweier Kinder. Sie war verheiratet, lebte jedoch getrennt. Ihren Lebensunterhalt verdiente sie zu dieser Zeit als Escort.


Beate Fischer kam am Morgen des 23. Juli 1994 von einer Feier. Unterwegs sprach sie eine Gruppe Nazis an, die sie aufforderten, mit ihnen zu kommen. Gemeinsam fuhren sie in die Wohnung eines der Nazis in der Emmentaler Straße, die seinerzeit Neonazis und rechten Skinheads als regelmäßiger Treffpunkt diente. Später behaupteten die Faschisten vor Gericht, Beate Fischer sei freiwillig mit ihnen gekommen. Eine Bekannte von Beate Fischer sagte jedoch in einer polizeilichen Vernehmung aus, sie würde Beate Fischer ein solches Verhalten nicht zutrauen, weil sie immer sehr vorsichtig gewesen sei und keine Sympathien für Rechte gehegt habe. Mehrfach versuchte Beate Fischer vergeblich, aus der Wohnung zu entkommen und die Täter davon zu überzeugen, sie freizulassen. Über zehn Stunden lang quälten die Nazis ihr Opfer, bevor sie Beate Fischer schließlich ermordeten.


Die Gewalt und der Sadismus, den die Faschisten an Beate Fischer auslebten, kamen nicht von ungefähr. author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Media groups decry harassment of journalists, activist during protest
content:
“Any act by law enforcement that prevents members of the press from documenting public assemblies undermines press freedom.”


CAGAYAN DE ORO — Several media organizations denounced the police harassment of photojournalists and an activist during a public demonstration in Pasay City on Wednesday, July 22.


In a statement, the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) said members of the Southern Police District allegedly arrested environmental activist and

Bulatlat

contributor Jian Sanz while taking photos during a mobilization in connection with the visit of United States State Secretary Marco Rubio in the country for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Foreign Ministers’ Meeting. 


Sanz said that the police prevented three women who were part of a paralegal team from entering the police station. However, lawyer Maria Sol Taule of the human rights alliance Karapatan came to her aid. Sanz was released after being detained for about 40 minutes. 


Videos that circulated online, on the other hand, showed that the police tried but failed to arrest photojournalists Bullit Marquez and Rene Dilan.


Police personnel attempt to arrest photojournalist Bullit Marquez during the protest action in connection with the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Pasay City on July 22, 2026. Screengrab from DZRH video report


In an

interview

 with DZRH News, Marquez said that he was prevented from taking photographs when the police attempted to arrest a protester, causing him to utter a cursed word. This led the police, Marquez said, to hold him. His camera fell to the ground as he resisted the attempt to arrest him.


NUJP reminded the Philippine National Police (PNP) of its role in ensuring the safety of media workers, as a stakeholder when the Philippine Plan of Action on the Safety of Journalists (PPASJ) was launched in 2019.


In April 2025, the PNP, in partnership with other government agencies, launched the PNP Media Security Vanguards program to enhance the safety and security of media practitioners.


“It is apparent that members of the PNP violate its own rules in dealing with members of the media,” NUJP said. “Unfortunately, today’s incident shows that elements of the PNP are themselves the perpetrators of attacks.”


The Photojournalists’ Center of the Philippines (PCP) condemned the harassment and intimidation, calling on the authorities to conduct an investigation and hold the responsible accountable. “Any act by law enforcement that prevents members of the press from documenting public assemblies undermines press freedom, the public’s right to information, and the principles of transparency and accountability.”


The Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP) and Press Photographers in the Philippines (PPP) also expressed their grave concerns about what happened.


According to The Philippine Star

report

, Pasay police chief Col. Joselito de Sesto called the attempted arrest of two photojournalists an “honest mistake,” as the police thought they were protesters.


PCP, however, said that Marquez was wearing his press credentials during the coverage.


For NUJP, the incident showed proof that the police do not understand the media’s role. “Why prevent journalists from covering a public interest event? Whose interest do you serve?”

(DAA)


The post

Media groups decry harassment of journalists, activist during protest

 appeared first on

Bulatlat

.

author: Equality Now
title: Survivors of sexual violence in South Asia struggle to access compensation, new report finds
content:
22nd July 2026


Survivors of sexual violence in South Asia struggle to access compensation, new report finds


10 min read


Press Releases


End sexual violence


Asia and the Pacific


A new report by SAMAJ reveals why many survivors of sexual violence in South Asia struggle to access financial compensation despite legal guarantees. 


Mumbai, India, July 22, 2026:

Beyond the devastating psychological and physical impacts, sexual violence often inflicts significant economic harm on survivors. While governments in South Asia have acknowledged this by establishing financial compensation schemes, new research finds that these systems are frequently underfunded, inconsistently implemented, and difficult to navigate, leaving many survivors unable to access the financial assistance they are legally entitled to.


These are just some of the findings of a new report,


The Good Practices Paper on

Compensation for Survivors of Sexual Violence in South Asia

, by the South Asian Movement for Accessing Justice (SAMAJ), a coalition of organisations working to end sexual violence in the region.


Why survivors of sexual violence struggle to access compensation 


Sexual violence often has long-lasting financial consequences. Survivors may face immediate out-of-pocket costs for emergency medical treatment, counselling, transport, legal assistance and, in some cases, relocation to escape further harm. Many are forced to take time off work or education, lose their livelihoods, or experience reduced earning potential because of the physical and psychological impacts. 


SAMAJ’s regional comparison of compensation schemes across Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and the Maldives finds survivors often face complex and lengthy criminal justice processes before they can access compensation. 


Long delays in investigations, trials, and administrative processes can leave survivors bearing the costs of pursuing justice while receiving little or no financial support when they need it most. A lack of awareness among both survivors and justice officials about compensation schemes,

low conviction rates for sexual violence

, and delays in the disbursement of funds are some of the other obstacles survivors face.


Where interim financial support is unavailable, survivors are often forced to choose between pursuing a lengthy and costly legal process they cannot afford or accepting an informal settlement, often under pressure. Coerced out-of-court settlements are widespread across South Asia, and the absence of emergency compensation is a significant factor driving survivors away from formal justice processes and allowing perpetrators to evade accountability. 


Compensation systems are failing survivors of sexual violence


In Pakistan, many survivors receive no compensation even after an offender has been convicted, because judges retain broad discretion over whether compensation is awarded, and many choose not to. 


In Bangladesh, courts awarded compensation in just 6.8% of reviewed rape cases, despite survivors’ legal entitlement to seek financial redress. The country also has no national victim compensation fund. 


Marginalised survivors of sexual violence face greater barriers to compensation


Dalit and Adivasi women, Indigenous women, religious minorities, and children born as a result of rape often face even greater obstacles. Discrimination, poverty, and social exclusion can make it harder to report sexual violence, be aware of legal rights, and navigate complex compensation processes. 


Women with disabilities face added challenges as justice officials often lack understanding of disability-related needs. Information about compensation schemes may be unavailable in accessible formats, while police stations, courts, and government offices are not always physically accessible.


Geographical barriers are particularly acute in the Maldives, an archipelago of around 200 inhabited islands. Forensic exam capacity, trained counsellors, shelters, and legal aid are concentrated in the capital, Malé, and just a few other urban centres. 


Several guidance notes for victims emphasise the need for rapid reporting to preserve forensic evidence. The island’s geography imposes logistical and cost barriers to the timely medical and forensic documentation that many compensation or assistance procedures require. Meanwhile, limited public data on compensation awards makes it difficult to assess whether compensation is reaching …

author: By Camilla Donzelli, Contributor
title: Inside Greece’s Refugee Camps, Gender-Based Violence Is Built Into the System
content:
Ritsona, Greece — Since 2022, the German collective Rosa Rolling Safespace has been providing a mobile safe space for women living in refugee camps around Athens. Their work shows that gender-based violence in these settings is not incidental but structural, a direct product of European and Greek migration policies.


Ritsona is a small town about 47 miles north of Athens. Driving through the surrounding countryside, it is hard to miss a sprawling cluster of gray containers encircled by barbed wire, surveillance cameras, and heavy metal gates monitored by police. It is one of the largest refugee camps in mainland Greece — according to

the latest data

 released by the Greek Ministry of Migration and Asylum, it has a nominal capacity of nearly 3,000 people.


Around the camp, hills and wind turbines stretch as far as the eye can see, occasionally interrupted by some industrial facilities breaking the monotony of the empty countryside. Once a week, however, a small dusty lot a few hundred meters from the camp’s main entrance comes to life.


Rosa Rolling Safespace setting up outside Ritsona camp. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


It is a Wednesday, and around midday two white vans appear at the far end of the long road running alongside the Ritsona camp. They park in the lot, and a group of about ten volunteers immediately get to work setting up a safe space for the women living inside.


Within half an hour, tables with hot and cold drinks, sewing machines, books, and children’s toys appear under a gazebo and a large yellow tent. The back of the larger van swings open, revealing a mobile medical clinic stocked with pads, tampons, and other essential supplies.


Medical truck brought to Ritsona camp by Rosa Rolling Safespace. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Medical truck with supplies brought to Ritsona camp by Rosa Rolling Safespace. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Sewing machines getting set up at Ritsona camp by volunteers from Rosa Rolling Safespace. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


The volunteers are part of

Rosa Rolling Safespace

, a self-funded German collective that has been operating in mainland Greece since 2022.


“The project started from the understanding that women experience different forms of violence,” said Ari, one of the volunteers. “Everyone who migrates is subjected to structural violence, but being a woman in this context adds specific layers.”


Every week, the vans travel between the camps of Ritsona, Malakasa, Oinofyta, and Thiva, all located in the greater Athens area. The collective provides mobile medical care, a community space, and a dedicated children’s area.


Ari explains that many women in the camps have no points of reference and often lack the time and energy to seek help when they need it. “The medical truck and the community space work together precisely for this reason,” she said. “Women come every week, sit down, talk with us. Our goal is to build trust, so they know there is a safe space they can always come back to if they need help.”


Rosa Rolling Safespace operates from a parking lot outside the camp partly as a deliberate political choice. “We don’t want to support this oppressive system,” said Ari. “We reject the way the European asylum system is designed and the effects it has on people. We don’t want to be complicit in it.”


Rosa Rolling Safespace set up outside Ritsona camp. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


But it is also a bureaucratic necessity. In 2020, the Greek government introduced

mandatory registration

 for organizations seeking to operate inside the camps. The process — costly and discretionary — effectively pushed out most independent groups, forcing them to work on the margins of the system. The result has been a double vacuum: fewer services for camp residents, and less independent monitoring of what happens inside.


This is not an accident. The current structure of refugee camps in Greece took shape with the EU’s

hotspot approach

, introduced in 2015 in response to arrivals by sea from Turkey. Originally designed as spaces for rapid identification and processing on the Aegean islands, hotspots gradually became containment facilities. 


In 2016, the

closure of borders

 by Macedonia, Croatia, and Slovenia left tens of thousands of people stranded in Greece, giving authorities a pretext to set up what were framed as emergency structures but have since become permanent.


The

EU-Turkey deal of March 2016 …
